claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game lacks any tutorial or guidance for learning basic mechanics.

citations.review_text:
This War of Mine is not about winning a war. It's about surviving one more night.

Instead of playing a soldier, you control ordinary civilians trapped in a city under siege. Every decision feels important: who gets food, who risks scavenging after dark, whether to help strangers, and how much of your humanity you're willing to sacrifice to survive.

The survival mechanics are simple to understand but emotionally brutal. Hunger, illness, depression, exhaustion, and constant shortages turn even small victories into meaningful achievements. Finding medicine for a sick survivor can feel more satisfying than winning an entire battle in most games.

The atmosphere is exceptional. The hand-drawn art style, haunting soundtrack, and bleak stories create a sense of desperation that few games manage to achieve. The added content in Final Cut further expands the experience with new stories, locations, and visual improvements.

It can be repetitive after many playthroughs, and the difficulty can sometimes feel unforgiving. That's also part of what makes the game so effective: survival is never guaranteed.

I began trying to optimize resources. I ended up questioning my moral compass because someone had canned food and I didn't.

I am so sorry, but even in a ruined city under constant siege, herbal medication is not worth more than a piece of family jewellery. I'm sorry it is just not. Real medication - fair enough, but herbal medication... Franko can stuff himself imo. 

Also the lack of tutorial in this game is a pain.

How is it that a game that is a decade old at this point and the first thing in the description is some bragging about how impressively remastered it is still sees fit to throw you in the middle of it without an explanation of literally anything? Not even the interface or the controls. At first I thought I was just dumb and missing something obvious, but no, there are other reviews complaining about the same problem.

This game is $20 but you are only able to play survival mode. Story mode and others all locked behind a DLC. There is no tutorial. As a new player this doesn't really feel good when you pay to play but then find out everything is locked behind a DLC.

Boring and repetitive. I felt like I had played the whole game after the 24 minutes. Given it another hour and a half to be sure and yup its the same simple loop over and over again. Game comes with no tutorial, no tips, no helpful info of any kind..... I think they are trying to make some statement about "the harsh reality of war" ok sure but you don't need any guidance because the game is so simple and so repetitive. I'm absolutely baffled by the extremely positive reviews this game has received

One of the best games you will never play yourself!

And for good reason...
No tutorial, no way to know which game mode is what, no way to know what you should do or what is actual progress. There is no way to stop the game to take a moment to get familiar with the mechanics. If you are meant to play the story mode first to get a tutorial, you are not guided to it. You have to assign each task to each survivor manually, can't move the camera to keep an eye on them and once they are done, they stand around as if they want to starve. Oh and each time you left click on the map by accident or to see if that is interactable, the character stops the current action and runs there. Usually ending up with them standing in front of a locked door and doing nothing while you wonder why the scavenger doesn´t continue,

The biggest war in "This war of mine" is trying to navigate the most basic controls you have ever seen in a game, without any chance to change buttons or inputs to those already limited controls. There are little to no shortcuts with buttons and the Action-Buttons are not explained, you have to guess what the "Hand-Symbol" does to every action. And on top of it, you have to micro-manage each task, are under constant pressure knowing it is an uphill battle, you are supposed to lear each time – AND YET THEY GIVE YOU NO TIME TO GET INTO THE GAME. You can not pause the game to read, you can not take your time to look at the characters to learn what illments come up.

The game is highly stylized to it's detriment: I have no way to enjoy the style of the game when I am frustrated because I misunderstood a game mechanic of a naked symbol with no way to see more about it. Make no mistake, I am proud to own this game and I will open it for a run and then forget about it again. 
To anyone who say that this is "realistic" or "immersive", to you I say to live in a war torn country if you need immersion. 

In the end, this game is worth existing and important to keep supportin…

I didn’t have high expectations for This War of Mine—just a bit curious— and was right. It ended up being quite boring. The game is a strategy survival title, but it doesn’t do a good job of explaining its mechanics, which makes it hard to really get into. Without a clear introduction or guidance, the gameplay feels slow and uneventful rather than engaging

If you’re interested in similar mechanics with more entertainment value, I’d suggest Fallout Shelter. It offers comparable resource management and strategy but is much more fun and approachable

For now, refunding
No tutorial, not even for basic interactions or game logic. Main menu makes it hard to understand which game mode to pick as a first timer. Don't waste your time here..
No tutorial? And full of ads for their DLCs? Wow.

Played, but mostly watched this quite a bit with a friend on mine that loves it, I really enjoy how you create an attachment to the characters and can easily create your own story, but, and this is merely a subjective opinion, never liked that much of the presentation and UI. Trying it now on the Deck lts very tyring to read the tiny text.

But in any case, this is one of the most realistic and original survival games out there.

Not my style. The controls are somewhat janky (you go from sneaking to running with the slightest push of the analog stick), there is no real tutorial, the game itself is depressing, you lose people quickly if you make a mistake. Text looks super small on my monitor.

I am sure I could 'git gud' and find a way to succeed in this game but it really provides me no incentive to. I don't like these vibes, Not because it's war, but because it's just not interesting in a narrative sense. Better controls, voiced dialogue, more story, and a tutorial would've gone a long way. This game gives me no real reason to care about my characters. This feels like it could be a mobile game.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game lacks a tutorial or explanatory text for its mechanics and combat system.

citations.review_text:
I had heard great things about this game and that everyone was raving about it when it came out. I decided to finally play it and initially I thought it was great. I like that the game is challenging and doesn't hold your hand. However, the lack of any kind of combat tutorial and seeming nonsensical game logic that I experienced has left a sour taste in my mouth.

I entered the Bakery with Katie and she was armed with a knife. While still in Scavenging mode, I opened a door and saw what looked to be a family of 3 (possibly a married couple and their in-law). They didn't exclaim at me so I walked through their room and didn't steal their things. As I went through the building I heard someone trying to pick the lock into the building and it sounded like they wanted to kill the man I saw earlier. I hid against the wall and two intruders entered the Bakery. I stealth killed the 2nd one and the 1st one turned around and attacked me (I guess he was too close to his friend?). 

The intruder suddenly had a knife icon that was half shaded and a circle around it. I thought I had to click this to attack him but clicking on it did nothing. I tried to click on my attacker and again nothing was happening and he continued to flay Katia into ribbons. Katia died and I was unable to attack the intruder. I was not in Scavenging mode as I clearly saw my knife was out. It was a frustrating moment since every survivor counts and since the game explains nothing, I feel like I'm being punished by the game. It would be one thing if I attacked someone and died, but I wasn't even able to attack back. Obviously I'm missing something but the game should clearly show the player what to do in combat as either a pop up or a tutorial of some kind. Survivors are everything in this game and to lose one due to a system that isn't clear at all is terrible.

To make matters worse, I sent another survivor to see if I could loot Katia and maybe get revenge on her killer. There was no sign of the kil…

A complicated recommendation. I think it delivers on its core premise really well, that of making morally complicated decisions and trying to survive in a war-torn area, and the art style is very in tune with this and done well. Fundamentally the game is good, but its execution leaves a lot to be desired. On sale though, it's an easy recommend. I'd also recommend reading the "Beginners Only Guide" in the Guides section of the Community Hub for the game, as there's no tutorial and the game can be outright frustrating to learn for no reason beyond the dev's meagre excuse that it's about 'realism'.

The survival mechanics are decently abstracted to make sense within the game, but also fall short in several ways. Firstly is probably a lack of depth in certain aspects: for example, every night when you have to choose between guarding, scavenging, and sleeping for your characters, you can only send one person out to scavenge. This sort of makes sense initially when you start with three of them, but with a fourth or even a fifth, there should have been the option to send multiple scavengers, especially as that would make sense to have someone on lookout on more dangerous sites. Scavenging is limited to the night, but regardless of how much time you use, you will always come back in the morning tired even if you finished up at 11pm, regardless of location, which feels a bit silly. At the very least, if they hadn't wanted multiple controlled characters in one salvage, let the player do multiple salvage runs per night.

There's a moral aspect where, depending on the character's background, they react in certain ways to decisions made. This can be buggy, such as reacting to stealing when nothing was stolen, but also annoying when it feels like it overreacts 40 days in to being attacked and having to kill someone, leading to depression while also saying that it was necessary?

And lastly is this 'gritty realism' that the developers seemingly went for. Nice on paper, but seems t…

No tutorial whatsoever, not even words. You have to figure out how the game works and what all the symbols mean by yourself with no so much as a label to help you. Glitchy symbols that don't always mean the same thing and show the wrong icon at times.

The game punishes you for playing it, making it absolutely no fun whatsoever. Doesn't matter what you do when the game decides randomly that you get raided, your people die and your stuff gets stolen even though you had guards with weapons and you have no control whatsoever over that aspect. The game just gives out bad moments constantly and you feel like you have no control, because you don't have control. The game just plays it's self and either it tells you that you win, or it tells you that you lose. Might as well flip a coin and keep your money.

IT IS NOT A GAME. IT IS AN EXPERIENCE. 

+ + + An experience about the cruelty of war. About the suffering and torment of ordinary civilians. Unfortunately, it is still a very relevant topic today.... 
Not a game you will find fun to play. But that is not its purpose. The devs made this game based on the personal stories of survivors of the blody Siege of Sarajevo. Strongly recommend. The first playthrough will hit.

+ + + Atmosphere is true art. The game has been remastered, so you can barely tell it is already 12 years old.

- - - The game will not tell you much about how to play. Also the combat system is not easy to learn. Charaters will die. Once you did 2-3 playthrough and played the DLC stories (very good ones) the game does not much to offer as you already know how everything works. 
It is not for everyone I know. Still a solid experience for only 3€ on sale. 

(I played it a lot 10 years ago and just got it on Steam as well. Definitely on my top 10 game list.)

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features a permadeath mechanic where a single mistake or character death ruins hours of progress and forces restarts.

citations.review_text: I don't like this game mechanic where you have to start all over again after failing once.

While This War of Mine features a beautifully crafted, immersive atmosphere, the actual gameplay loop falls flat. Scavenging and cooking quickly become tedious, and the permadeath mechanic means a single mistake can ruin hours of progress. The pacing is particularly frustrating: because the game pauses when you alt-tab and lacks a fast-forward feature, you are forced to stare at the screen while characters sleep. Skipping to the end of the day isn't a viable solution either, as it risks missing crucial random events like traders or neighbors asking for help. It is a valiant attempt at a serious survival experience, but the disrespect for the player's time makes it hard to recommend.

The game's atmosphere and premise are very well-crafted and immersive but the gameplay loop of scavenging and cooking food isn't really that interesting to me. It gets stale quickly and one mistake can pretty much end your run which sucks quite a bit.

claims.claim: Reviewers state that the game lacks a fast-forward feature and forces players to wait through periods where characters sleep or perform slow actions.

Scavenging and cooking quickly become tedious, and the permadeath mechanic means a single mistake can ruin hours of progress. The pacing is particularly frustrating: because the game pauses when you alt-tab and lacks a fast-forward feature, you are forced to stare at the screen while characters sleep. Skipping to the end of the day isn't a viable solution either, as it risks missing crucial random events like traders or neighbors asking for help. The game's mechanics are fun but it leans too far into art-house in an effort to force the 'realism of boredom' by not allowing you to speed time up - it gets truly lame just watching your exhausted house all sleep for half a day.  The UX also needs lots of love: why does it default to destroying furniture if you have an ax in your inventory?, why are the build vs. items in your inventory supplies displayed backwards?, there's so many more examples.

This game has a lot of potential to be a survival experience game but there's so many frustrating moments that I think it fails to rise to the challenge of the tone / backdrop.  Valiant attempt but not worth the time in my experience.

Can't say it's bad, but I don't think it's for me - the combination of slow pace and high stakes is not something I like. Some things are unrealistic enough to pull me out of the game: you cannot scavenge with more than one person, making bandages requires pure alcohol and herbs, you cannot disassemble large furniture to make fuel, you cannot boil water to purify it. Also the controls - mouse drags move the screen but clicks direct the characters, so it's way to easy to accidentally send a person somewhere while scrolling the map. Some actions take away your characters for the whole day, even when the description sounds easy. And so on.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe combat and engagements as awkward and lacking fluid control.

citations.review_text:
Fun and interesting game, I think some mechanics aren't communicated well (like depression or value of items) but I appreciate what the game tries to do. Stealth is really promoted here because the "gameplay" blows chunks and you really don't wanna get caught out in an engagement, awkward animations and not fluid encounters if you are getting shot or your ass beat. The game can feel punishing if you try to explore because the gameplay is so awkward, there is no confidence when entering combat unless you have a gun, which is still a decent chance for you to mess up. The characters are meaningfully different from each other and I like how they communicate. The overall message of the story and just trying to survive everyday is very impactful and nudges the ever present, deeply rooted question of war and conflict. 

"Why would someone do this?"

I appreciate the ability to modify a run as well, choosing your characters, timeline, and location. It adds replay value without diminishing the things that make this game fun. The game is difficult, highlighting the harshness of the world, eventually you'll get into an end game groove but winter will push your ♥♥♥♥ in. Game goes on sale often, buy then.

This War of Mine is a game attempting to bridge survival gaming with linear story telling. In this game you play various survivors in scenarios where they must scavenge, defend a shelter and craft workstation and tools to survive. There are numerous problems on display with this title. Whether you look at the mechanics or the story telling, there is simply too much botched jobs around it.

The presentation of the game is superb. The comic book ink style presentation works amazingly well. The environments in which the scenes happen are only flawed by perpetual animations, which end up making no sense. You can certainly forget about coherence while navigating the maps. That said, you can soon figure out the game was never really intended to be more than its presentation.

You prepare meals, there is a timer for the activity. It takes one hour. Then you painstakingly select another character, which is always a pain. Selecting and deselecting characters is awful. You send one character to the basement, while another is cooking. One hour later, the character still hasn't made it to the basement, but meanwhile another gentleman had time to chop up a grand wardrobe. It makes NO sense. The time management is completely botched up. You start right-clicking to make everyone run, it's still a stupid pain. The characters don't need to have excuses to not execute the commands you put up. Some times they do have valid issues, but most of the time not. So you end up spamming right-clicking all the time.

Fortunately, that's only half the game. The other half is spent scavenging various scenes which appear randomly on the map, selected at the beginning of each game. Very few characters are actually good at scavenging. That gives the RNG a perfect angle to screw your runs up. Also fortunately, the game only saves at the beginning of the day, giving you perfect excuses to just restart trying every destination to find out if the RNG is screwing you up. claims.claim: Reviewers report that characters can accidentally break down their own built furniture because the game interface struggles to distinguish between custom-built structures and junk.

citations.review_text:
First of, it's not a bad game. It has basic mechanics, and it can be fun playing for a bit.
But, unfortunately, it has several bugs and issues that are incredibly easy to fix and yet the developers show no interest addressing. 
Mainly, the game loses sound if you step away from the computer and come back in a few minutes. Then you have to either play without sound, which really sucks, or lose all your progress and quit the game. No other game has ever done this in decades of playing thousands of games. 
Then you scape together your little resources you have to build something, only for an icon to pop up - hey come here, break this down for free wood scraps. So you accidentally keep breaking your own furniture because the game is not smart enough to distinguish between junk and what you build. 
It's a game with promising mechanics, but the user experience is atrocious at best. No queuing of orders, or knowing stats of anything. There is too much running around endlessly, doing the same thing over and over.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that inventory stacking limits restrict players to carrying very small amounts of certain items like screws and bolts.

citations.review_text:
Although I only have 22 hours in my steam library, I have hundreds if not possibly a thousand hours on my mobile devices and tablets collectively playing the games through the years and the dlcs. 
I love the game and was extremely surprised when I first got it. I thought it was going to be a pov from a over the shoulder experience, but having a hallowed house and foggy rooms behind unknown doors was a whole game changer. And actually kinda drew me closer to the game.  I played several scenarios and different levels doing my best to keep everyone alive and happy, but also understanding the situation happening outside in the war torn streets .. the stories are well written and I remember most letters like if I put them in my jacket myself.  

The levels are decently balanced once you figure out what you need to build and do and collect. 

The only issue I can think of is the stacking of items . Not saying bigger backpack but carry more than 6 screws and bolts and some other items? I can shove a handful in my bag or jacket pocket and not be over encumbered 

What you need is something like a tutorial. To help players understand the game. Have people in a house that has most of the equipment that you need to survive so they can understand what does what and what you can build and cook, but soldiers raid the house for the equipment, while they are distracted the survivors make a run for it... Starting the story at a bare house.


But overall WONDERFUL GAME ❣️

What can I say.... this was the first time i ever played a game like this. (more into starcraft, total war , warhammer, fps etc games) and was absolutely instantly hooked. Its a playstyle I never encountered before but easily able too figure out. The style of choosing too be good or evil, or too steal/not steal, kill/leave alive. all the while has base building in it also. I highly suggest watching gameplay online because reading another persons review on it can only go so far. but IMO buy it. claims.claim: Reviewers report technical issues when alt-tabbing out of the game, including sound loss and forced pausing even in windowed mode.

citations.review_text:
First of, it's not a bad game. It has basic mechanics, and it can be fun playing for a bit.
But, unfortunately, it has several bugs and issues that are incredibly easy to fix and yet the developers show no interest addressing. 
Mainly, the game loses sound if you step away from the computer and come back in a few minutes. Then you have to either play without sound, which really sucks, or lose all your progress and quit the game. No other game has ever done this in decades of playing thousands of games. 
Then you scape together your little resources you have to build something, only for an icon to pop up - hey come here, break this down for free wood scraps. So you accidentally keep breaking your own furniture because the game is not smart enough to distinguish between junk and what you build. 
It's a game with promising mechanics, but the user experience is atrocious at best. No queuing of orders, or knowing stats of anything. There is too much running around endlessly, doing the same thing over and over.
The game keeps pausing when alt-tab even if you play in window mode. I tried everything and couldn't find a solution. Avoid it if you enjoy or need multitasking while playing.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game lacks an in-game speed control option and does not provide an introduction or tutorial when starting out.

citations.review_text:
Pros: Excellent re-playability, convincing and compelling atmosphere. Graphics that perfectly match the setting and environment. Great and memorable soundtrack. Amazing story telling through small notes and character monologues. Realistic combat / exploration system.
Cons: Inability to increase / reduce in-game speed.

This game is amazing. I find myself continually coming back to it. 

As a new player, it is clever to not give any introduction. What is the value of an item? Who knows? There is no tutorial level for a civilian during wartime, and this game puts you right into it. 

As you continue to play, you ask questions of morality and ethics. Is it ethical to steal from the old couple to feed the children? So often games paint morality into such black and white choices, but this game lives in the grey. And as you play and become more and more desperate, you find yourself making more and more difficult ethical decisions. You really see how some people can come to commit horrific acts during wartime just to survive.

claims.claim: Reviewers highlight that once players learn the map locations and mechanics, the game loses its initial challenge and becomes too easy.

citations.review_text:
An absolute gem worth every penny you'd spend on it.

Gameplay-wise, it's great. One of, if not the best base manager I can think of. Tough, but fair early game, where you don't rely on RNG to find the necessary goods, you're just barely surviving by design. Mid-game is lovely, since there's always something requiring you to think hard about what you'll do, as winter is coming, bandits will get bold and start raiding you more often, the fightings between rebels and soldiers will become more intense restricting your looting and so on and so forth. And since most scenarios end after 35-50 days, you'll never really relax up until the end. As for the exploration at night, it's absolutely lovely as well, with a large variety of locations and various scenarios for many of them. My only real complaint is caused purely by how good I am at the game already, clearing bandit hideouts usually has no morale penalty and these locations are filled to brim with loot, which you can then trade, trivializing the game, but that's why I tend to give myself a self-imposed challenge to not abuse that fact.

Story/character-wise, Christ, this is the only game off the top of my head that has us play as civilians during the war. I love how you'll have to genuinely consider stealing or even killing other civilians for the sake of your own survival (unless, again, you know how to clear bandit hideouts), the game often puts you into such tough spots. How much charity can you afford? How much are you willing to risk? Also, the majority of the characters have some niche, they differ enough to offer unique approach to the exact same gameplay loop. So on a Bruno/Roman/Arica run, you'll need to play to play into your strengths, so steal and fight, since this is what your characters excel at and all are rather indifferent to being cruel, while on a Boris/Emilia/Marin run, you'll rely on Boris, easily depressed, but an excellent scavanger. The DLCs are mostly great as well, forsaking some gameplay ele…

I rarely feel that everyone should try a game, but this is one of those cases. In terms of raising awareness, I couldn't think of a better example that captures the hopeless atmosphere of modern warfare. I truly feel that it makes you a better person and changes the way you view wars and the civilians caught up in them, especially nowadays, when wars still poison our everyday lives. Besides, it's so refreshing to play a war game where we're not heroic soldiers. This is a beautiful game, and 11 bit studios deserves all the respect it gets. In 2022, they organized a fundraiser for Ukrainian refugees and released a special DLC, the proceeds of which went to help civilians. In terms of gameplay, I can imagine that some people will find it boring or too difficult, but this is not a game for everyone. It requires the right attitude and mood. I can only think of one negative: once you get to know the mechanics, it doesn't really offer any kind of challenge, and you'll be able to play through it without any problems as many times as you want. But maybe that's not such a negative thing here. It's meant to convey a feeling and a message rather than provide a Dark Souls experience. In summary, this is a work of art that transcends its status as a game and does so for a good cause. 10/10

claims.claim: Reviewers praise the game's atmosphere, noting its somber soundtrack, distinct art style, and emotional storytelling centered on civilians during wartime.

citations.review_text:
Love this game. It is challenging but rewarding. The music is stunning and fits the atmosphere well. I still get antsy when listening to "No Good Choice". Don't buy This war of mine if you can't handle dying because it will happen A LOT. 

I recommend to go in blind so don't search for tips/walkthroughs before playing your first rounds unless you really need it <3

Very creative art style and gameplay experience! While most other games about war focuses on the people fighting it on the front lines, this is a welcome break from that, focusing on those caught up in it and trying to survive/

The nitty gritty art style really fits for this purpose, as you'll quickly find out that, no matter which character or scenario you choose, its a grim affair. In fact, very often there is no true happy ending at all, and the best u can hope for is something bittersweet.

Its a dose of realism that I don't often see and is greatly appreciated. This War of Mine really captures the feeling of hopelessness so well as someone who is trapped in a war zone, not knowing when they're going to run out of food and water. 

There's also a lot of differences between the characters as well, and some of the scenarios are especially challenging because of this. Each has their strengths and weaknesses u have to deal with. Christo for instance needs much less sleep and has good carrying capacity, but he comes with his daughter Iskra, who starts off being a depressed and complete liability that u have to manage.

Gameplay wise, its a surprisingly fun and challenging point and click scavenging adventure. Early on, things are easy, but they quickly escalate in difficulty. And I don't just mean in terms of meeting hostile enemies who will kill u on sight (including 1 psycho who will chase u around the map if she even spots u), but also in terms of balancing hard moral choices.

Do I rob the old, defenseless couple to get some medicine I need? Or do I leave them alone and hope I can find another source later that doesn't involve dooming others to death from illness or starvation?

This isn't just something u have to face, but also something u see others in the game face as well. Sometimes you'll come across the remains of what someone else did just to survive, but other times it plays out in front of u and u have to decide whether to try and intervene or use someo…

Years after playing it, i still think of the intense atmosphere of this game. The music, the graphic, the hard decisions you will make - all blend into a great game experience. A raw feeling, that no other game gave me.

This War of Mine was one of the first games I got on Steam almost 10 years ago, and the concept hit me instantly. We are used to seeing combat and FPS, but I had never seen a game that seeks to portray how it feels for the rest of the people, those who live around the conflict and are stuck there with no way out.
As someone who has never been even close to a war zone, I have no idea if this is realistic or not. All I know is that it made me care about the characters, feel their struggles, worry about their well-being and hope for the end.
In this game, the same moral decisions carried weight they didn't in other scenarios. The game deeply humanizes its characters, and you see the "villains" stand in a grey moral area: people who do bad things, not because they are mean or evil, but because they are selfish, they are desperate, they want to survive. You get to know the characters, their stories, understand their morals and the impact every decision has on each one.
The art in this game also does an amazing job of conveying the tragic scenario. The music is somber, the drawings have rough edges, and it works perfectly for the depressing atmosphere. But there are also gleams of hope: you can hear soft music on the radio, kids laughing when they are happy.
I never had issues with bugs in the game that bothered the playing experience. The UI is simple, resources are scarce, and the winter is relentless. You do what you can, but it shows how easy it is for someone in a bad situation to end up in one even worse: an untreated cold or a small wound can become deadly. The days can be monotonous, the nights are tense, the work gets repetitive, but I like it. It pays off when your characters are safe and fed.
This is what matters most. It's a game that really goes for feelings, so you have to feel how everything is deliberate and reflect on what it means. That is the experience This War of Mine brings. And this is why I keep coming back to it. When you start to become numb to t…

claims.claim: Reviewers report encountering technical issues such as application crashes on startup and bugs involving NPC scripting or pathfinding.

citations.review_text:
I quit because I got tired of putting up with bugs.

This War of Mine deliberately restricts saving so you have to live with the consequences of your choices. That only works if the game itself is reliable.

It isn't. Bugs and broken NPC scripting can create permanent consequences the player never chose, and the game gives you no way to undo them. In a game built around morality and irreversible decisions, that is a fundamental design failure.

I don't mind harsh consequences when they're caused by my decisions. I do mind being permanently punished for the game's bugs.

The game is still full of bugs after over 10 years. It'll never be fixed.

Not recommended.
